key_terms.meaning: Sender and receiver encrypt and decrypt with the same secret key, so the key must be shared before use
C = M ⊕ K with a random key K as long as the message M, used once, giving perfect secrecy
The secret key itself must be delivered over a channel an eavesdropper may be watching
Bennett–Brassard 1984 scheme: the key is sent as single qubits in the Z or X basis, randomly chosen per bit
Entanglement-based QKD where Alice and Bob share Bell pairs and test a Bell (CHSH) inequality to detect an eavesdropper
Alice and Bob publicly compare only their basis choices and keep the bit positions where the bases matched
Fraction of the sifted key bits on which Alice and Bob disagree; a value above roughly 11% signals an eavesdropper
No unitary can copy an arbitrary unknown qubit, so |ψ⟩|0⟩ cannot be mapped to |ψ⟩|ψ⟩ for all |ψ⟩
H(X) = −Σ pₓ log₂ pₓ, the average number of bits needed to describe the outcome of X
S(ρ) = −Tr(ρ log₂ ρ), equal to the Shannon entropy of the eigenvalues of the density matrix ρ
n copies of a pure-state source with entropy S can be compressed to about nS qubits and recovered faithfully
χ = S(Σ pᵢ ρᵢ) − Σ pᵢ S(ρᵢ), the upper bound on classical information readable from an ensemble of quantum states
The pattern of parity-check outcomes that identifies which error has occurred, without revealing the codeword
A k-dimensional subspace of n-bit strings with minimum Hamming distance d between codewords
Encoding |0⟩ → |000⟩ and |1⟩ → |111⟩ so that a single X error can be located and undone
Concatenation of the three-qubit phase-flip and bit-flip codes; it corrects any single-qubit error on one of nine physical qubits
Measuring operators such as Z₁Z₂ and Z₂Z₃ to get error information while leaving the encoded logical values untouched
A logical gate built by applying the same physical gate bit-by-bit across the code block, so one fault stays on one qubit
If the physical error rate per gate and per time step is below a constant threshold, arbitrarily long reliable quantum computation is possible with enough encoding

takeaways: Private-key cryptography is only as strong as the secrecy of the shared key, so the key distribution step is the real target for an attacker.
BB84 and E91 make eavesdropping detectable because an unknown quantum state cannot be measured or copied without disturbing it.
Classical information counts bits and is bounded by Shannon entropy; quantum information counts qubits and is bounded by von Neumann entropy.
No-cloning and disturbance are extra quantum constraints that have no classical counterpart and change what an eavesdropper can do.
Shannon's theorem sets the compression limit H(X) for classical data, and Schumacher's theorem sets the limit S(ρ) for quantum data.
The Holevo quantity limits how many classical bits a quantum ensemble can carry, even when the states are not orthogonal.
A classical code stores a message in a subspace and uses syndrome measurements to locate and undo errors without reading the message.
A quantum code hides one logical qubit in entangled physical qubits and measures only stabilizers, never the amplitudes of the encoded state.
The three-qubit code fixes bit flips, the nine-qubit code fixes both bit and phase flips, and fault-tolerant design keeps one physical fault from becoming a logical error.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for the full BB84 steps with sifting and QBER, the entropy definitions with a small numerical calculation, a code example worked through syndrome decoding, and the threshold theorem with its practical meaning.

bank.q: Explain private-key cryptography, describe the one-time pad, and show why the one-time pad is perfectly secure but still fails in practice.
outline: Encryption C = M ⊕ K with the same secret key K for both sides
One-time pad is perfectly secure because for any ciphertext every plaintext stays equally likely
Key must be truly random, as long as the message, and used only once
The real weakness is distributing K over a channel the enemy may read
Names the key distribution problem that QKD later solves

bank.q: Describe the BB84 quantum key distribution protocol step by step and explain how Alice and Bob end up with a shared secret key.
outline: Alice sends one photon per bit, randomly in Z basis (|0⟩, |1⟩) or X basis (|+⟩, |−⟩)
Bob measures each photon in a basis he picks at random
Sifting: public comparison of bases only, keeping matching positions
Error estimation on a sample of the sifted key, then reconciliation and privacy amplification
Any measurement by Eve disturbs the states and raises the QBER

bank.q: Explain the E91 entanglement-based key distribution scheme and how a Bell inequality test reveals an eavesdropper.
outline: Source produces Bell pairs, one qubit to Alice, one to Bob
Measurements along chosen directions give correlated outcomes
Testing the CHSH quantity S; quantum mechanics allows S up to 2√2, any local hidden-variable model gives S ≤ 2
Eavesdropping changes the observed correlations and drives S down towards the classical bound
Remaining correlated pairs give the key

bank.q: Compare classical and quantum information theory under the headings: unit of information, measure of uncertainty, copying, and disturbance on measurement.
outline: Bit versus qubit; classical state is definite, qubit can be in superposition or entangled
Shannon entropy H(X) versus von Neumann entropy S(ρ), with S(ρ) = H of the eigenvalues of ρ
Classical bits copy freely; no-cloning forbids copying an unknown qubit
Classical measurement can be passive in principle; quantum measurement disturbs non-orthogonal states
Consequence: no unconditional security by copying, but eavesdropping becomes detectable

bank.q: State and explain Shannon's noiseless channel coding theorem and Schumacher's noiseless channel coding theorem.
outline: Shannon: n independent outcomes of X can be compressed to about nH(X) bits and recovered with vanishing error
H(X) = −Σ pₓ log₂ pₓ; typical sequences carry almost all the probability
Converse: fewer than nH(X) bits cannot work reliably
Schumacher: n copies of a pure-state source with density matrix ρ compress to about nS(ρ) qubits
S(ρ) = −Tr(ρ log₂ ρ); compression is a unitary on the typical subspace

bank.q: A source emits four symbols with probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.125. Compute the Shannon entropy and state the compression limit for one million symbols.
outline: H = 1.75 bits per symbol
One million symbols need about 1.75 × 10⁶ bits = 1.75 Mbit, not 2 Mbit
Compression exists because the four symbols are not equally likely

bank.q: Alice sends the bits 01101 using BB84 with bases Z, X, X, Z, Z and Bob measures with bases Z, Z, X, Z, X. Find the sifted key and explain what happens to the discarded bits.
outline: Compare bases position by position: match at positions 1, 3, 4
Positions 2 and 5 are discarded
Sifted key is the bits at the matching positions, in order
Discarded bits are never used because Bob's measurement basis was wrong
Note that the discarded bits are still used later in the protocol for security checks

bank.q: A density matrix in its eigenbasis is diag(1/2, 1/4, 1/4). Compute the von Neumann entropy and state what it means for Schumacher compression.
outline: S(ρ) = −Σ λᵢ log₂ λᵢ with λᵢ = 1/2, 1/4, 1/4
S(ρ) = 1.5 bits per qubit
n copies compress to about 1.5n qubits
Equality holds because ρ is diagonal in the given basis, so eigenvalues are the diagonal entries

bank.q: Using the three-qubit bit-flip code with |0⟩ → |000⟩ and |1⟩ → |111⟩, show how the syndrome measurement Z₁Z₂ and Z₂Z₃ locates a single X error and corrects it.
outline: Encode a logical state α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ as α|000⟩ + β|111⟩
Error X on qubit 2 gives α|010⟩ + β|101⟩
Measure Z₁Z₂ and Z₂Z₃: outcomes give the syndrome, e.g. (−1, −1) for an error on qubit 2
Syndrome table: (+,+) no error, (−,+) qubit 1, (−,−) qubit 2, (+,−) qubit 3
Apply X to the flagged qubit; amplitudes α and β are never measured

bank.q: A linear code has parity-check matrix H. Explain how the syndrome s = Hr is computed for a received word r and how a single-bit error is found from a lookup table.
outline: Write r = c + e with c a codeword and e the error pattern
Syndrome s = Hr = Hc + He = He because Hc = 0 for every codeword
Build a table mapping each single-bit error to its syndrome (a column of H)
Match s to the table, flip the identified bit
Corrects all single errors when the columns of H are nonzero and distinct

bank.q: Explain why the no-cloning theorem is essential for the security of quantum key distribution, and what would go wrong if perfect cloning were possible.
outline: State the theorem: no unitary copies an arbitrary unknown |ψ⟩
An eavesdropper cannot copy the intercepted qubit and forward the original undisturbed
Without cloning, Eve must measure, which disturbs non-orthogonal states and raises the QBER
If cloning existed, Eve could keep a copy, wait for basis announcement, and measure perfectly
Hence no-cloning turns an attack into a detectable disturbance

bank.q: Explain the Holevo bound and use it to discuss how much classical information can be read from a noisy quantum channel.
outline: An ensemble {pᵢ, ρᵢ} carries at most χ = S(Σpᵢρᵢ) − ΣpᵢS(ρᵢ) bits per use
For n uses the accessible information is bounded by nχ
Orthogonal states reach χ = H(X); non-orthogonal states fall short
Classical capacity of a quantum channel maximised over input ensembles; Holevo–Schumacher–Westmoreland theorem
Practical reading: quantum channels can carry classical data, but the bound can be below the qubit count

bank.q: Compare the three-qubit bit-flip code and the nine-qubit Shor code, and justify why nine qubits are needed to handle an arbitrary single-qubit error.
outline: Three-qubit code corrects X only; a Z error maps |000⟩ to |000⟩ and |111⟩ to −|111⟩, invisible to the code
Phase flips must be caught in the Hadamard (X-basis) frame — the three-qubit phase-flip code
A general single-qubit error is a combination of X and Z (with Y = iXZ), so both must be corrected
The nine-qubit code concatenates the two codes: three blocks of three
Syndromes separate which block has a phase flip and which qubit has a bit flip, giving distance 3 and correcting any one-qubit error

bank.q: Explain the fault-tolerant threshold theorem, the role of transversal gates and syndrome extraction, and why the result matters for building a large quantum computer.
outline: Fault tolerance: one physical fault must cause at most one error in the logical block
Transversal gates act bit-by-bit across blocks so errors do not spread within a block
Syndrome extraction repeated with verified ancillas; errors in the ancilla must not leak into the data
Threshold theorem: below a constant physical error rate, concatenation or surface codes make the logical error rate arbitrarily small
Cost is polylogarithmic overhead in the number of physical qubits per logical qubit
Practically, hardware must beat the threshold before large algorithms become reliable

glossary.def: A classical two-state unit that holds exactly 0 or 1.
A two-level quantum system whose state is a unit vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ in a two-dimensional Hilbert space.
A positive operator with trace 1 that describes a quantum state, including statistical mixtures.
H(X) = −Σ pₓ log₂ pₓ, the average uncertainty in bits about the outcome of a random variable X.
S(ρ) = −Tr(ρ log₂ ρ), the quantum version of Shannon entropy equal to the entropy of the eigenvalues of ρ.
H(X,Y) for a pair of variables, measuring uncertainty about both together.
I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X,Y), the information that Y carries about X.
There is no unitary that maps |ψ⟩|0⟩ to |ψ⟩|ψ⟩ for every unknown state |ψ⟩.
The maximum classical information per channel use, χ = S(Σ pᵢ ρᵢ) − Σ pᵢ S(ρᵢ).
The largest mutual information between the input symbol and the outcome of the best measurement on the output state.
Compression of n copies of a pure-state source to about nS(ρ) qubits with fidelity approaching 1.
Encryption C = M ⊕ K with a random key K as long as the message, used once.
The adversary in a key distribution protocol who tries to learn the key without being detected.
The step in BB84 where Alice and Bob keep only the bits for which their basis choices agree.
The fraction of sifted key bits where Alice and Bob disagree, used to bound eavesdropper information.
Hashing the partly secret raw key into a shorter key about which the eavesdropper has almost no information.
The number of positions in which two binary strings differ.
A set of codewords forming a vector space over GF(2), described by a generator matrix G and parity-check matrix H.
A matrix whose rows define the parity checks; a word r is a codeword exactly when Hr = 0.
The vector s = Hr computed from a received word; it depends only on the error, not on the message.
The protected qubit carried by an entangled block of physical qubits in a quantum error-correcting code.
A quantum code defined as the simultaneous +1 eigenspace of a set of commuting Pauli operators.
A logical operation applied as the same physical gate on each qubit of a code block, preventing error spread.
The result that below a constant physical error rate per gate, arbitrarily long fault-tolerant quantum computation is possible with extra encoding.
